title: The role of the astronaut is in flux
gist: Reviewing three new books after Artemis II, the essay argues that human spaceflight's many justifications are downstream of a primal instinct to roam, that a small group of nations and billionaires is deciding the off-Earth future, and that a new US–China lunar resource race is reshaping the astronaut's role from Cold War symbol to commercial pilgrim.

insights.claim: A slew of new books argues that all rationales for human spaceflight—prestige, science, business—are downstream of a basic evolutionary instinct to expand and adapt that may need no rational explanation.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: If the driver is primal rather than economic, spaceflight demand may persist regardless of near-term return-on-investment math.
insights.quote: Humans have itchy feet, and we are simply wired to roam.
insights.locator: In the wake of Artemis II

insights.claim: It remains unclear whether launching humans into space delivers a better return on investment than sending robots to make scientific discoveries or conduct commercial activities like mining.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: The unresolved robots-versus-humans ROI question is the core cost-justification risk hanging over crewed-mission budgets.
insights.quote: Launching humans into space is dangerous and expensive, and it’s unclear whether it can deliver a better return on investment than we’d get if we were to send robots in our stead

insights.claim: Anthropologist Deana Weibel frames human space exploration as an extension of the ancient compulsion to embark on perilous pilgrimages in order to experience revelations about the universe.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: The pilgrimage frame explains persistent demand for civilian spaceflight beyond utilitarian value.
insights.locator: Indeed, in her new book, The Ultraview Effect

insights.claim: The Artemis program aims to establish a US-led human base on the moon's south pole in the 2030s, while China and Russia plan their own crewed lunar base in the same region on a similar timeline.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: Overlapping bases in the same resource-rich region set up direct geopolitical competition over a contested zone.

insights.claim: Leroy Chiao argues the new space race's first-place prize is uncontested access to valuable resources such as water from ice patches on the moon's south pole, unlike the Cold War contest over symbolic dominance.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: Reframes lunar competition as resource-driven, implying commercial and strategic stakes beyond prestige.
insights.quote: the new first-place prize could be uncontested access to valuable resources such as water
insights.locator: NASA is, however, making an overt case

insights.claim: Space law prohibits any nation from owning part of the moon, but a first-mover advantage may accrue to whoever sets up on the most resource-rich patches even without official ownership, and nuclear-reactor exclusion zones will effectively partition territory.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: De facto occupation via exclusion zones could route around ownership treaties, a legal-gray-area risk for space governance.
insights.quote: These outposts will inevitably be powered by nuclear reactors, so safety will require exclusion zones around them.
insights.locator: Space law prohibits any nation from owning part of the moon

insights.claim: A relatively small group of players—with SpaceX CEO Elon Musk the most conspicuous example—currently has an outsize role in determining the path of human spaceflight.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: Concentration of decision power in a few billionaires and states is the governance risk the essay urges the public to contest.
insights.quote: a relatively small group of players in human spaceflight have an outsize role in determining the path forward
insights.locator: At the moment, a relatively small group

insights.claim: Blue Origin has ferried more than 80 civilians on brief suborbital flights, including William Shatner, Katy Perry, and cardiologist Eiman Jahangir, while Musk wants SpaceX to launch millions into orbit and settle Mars.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: Concrete traction in space tourism signals a maturing commercial market even amid doubts about grander visions.
insights.locator: Blue Origin, the company founded by Jeff Bezos

insights.claim: The intense online backlash to the all-female April 2025 Blue Origin celebrity mission, mocked despite its feminist branding, hints that who gets to go to space and how may inspire growing acrimony as flights become common.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: Public discomfort with commodified spaceflight is a reputational headwind for space-tourism marketing.

themes.theme: The ultraview effect and human witness

insights.claim: Weibel's 'ultraview effect' inverts the overview effect, turning the astronaut's gaze outward into the universe's immensity to produce awe tempered by alienation and what Burke called 'delightful horror.'
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: A new psychological framing for the value of human presence in space, distinct from utilitarian arguments.
insights.quote: when we realize the extent of the vast mysteries we are not equipped to understand

insights.claim: Robotic probes are humanity's most daring emissaries and may outlive us, but people identify with space only when a human is out there doing it, so both are needed.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: The enduring public pull toward human witness sustains crewed-mission demand even where robots are cheaper and safer.
insights.quote: People identify when there’s a human out there doing it.
insights.locator: But while these spacecraft are our scouts

insights.claim: It wasn't until astronaut Bill Anders snapped the 'Earthrise' shot on Apollo 8 that lunar-orbit views of Earth hit home for the public, and Artemis II astronaut photos went similarly viral.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: Human-taken imagery drives public engagement that robotic imagery does not, a soft asset for crewed-program funding.

insights.claim: Leroy Chiao contends that deliverance in space is a mirage and finds comfort in the idea that humanity, like every group of intelligent life, has its own cycle and that it is okay to be extinct.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: A veteran astronaut rejecting the species-survival rationale challenges the existential marketing behind Mars settlement.
insights.quote: We’re not in this race to save ourselves.

insights.claim: Many skeptics in the legal, political, financial, and public spheres doubt that a thriving market for space resources will materialize in the near term.
insights.speaker: Becky Ferreira
insights.so_what: Near-term commercial doubt is a check on the resource-race investment thesis driving lunar plans.
